title: Sandbox POC Blueprint — Lightweight Adapter Patterns & Live-debug Cheatsheet
content:
Purpose and context:
This doc is a compact, field-ready blueprint for running a short (2–4 hour) customer-facing sandbox POC that focuses on: lightweight adapter patterns, live-debug workflows, and quick experiments with routing / kv-cache prefetch behavior. Its intended for Solutions Engineering (SE) pairs running an on-site or remote workshop where the customer needs to validate a deployment approach end-to-end without committing to Dedicated capacity or a full Private rollout.

When to use this blueprint:
- Customer wants a fast proof that an LLM feature can be integrated into their microservices without heavy infra changes.
- Need to demonstrate graceful fallback between model variants or regions.
- Validate KV prefix caching effects on latency/cost for a chat-style product.

Prereqs (what SE should prepare ahead of the session):
- Sandbox project in Redwood Console with ephemeral API key and a small usage quota.
- Minimal sample microservice repo forked from the workspace-adapter-template (link in linked_artifacts).
- Prebuilt docker image for the adapter (tag: se-sandbox-lite:latest) pushed to our internal registry.
- A short curated prompt set and 10 synthetic chat traces that reflect customer payload shapes.
- Local laptop with Docker/WSL + kubectl installed and kubeconfig pointing to the workshop namespace.
- Optional: a low-cost test instance for Private mode (if customer requests VPC demo).

Lab objectives and success criteria (for a 3-hour session):
1) Deploy an adapter that proxies requests to Redwoods hosted API and returns structured responses. Success: adapter running locally or on k8s and returning valid JSON 95% of the time for sample prompts.
2) Toggle between two model variants (fast/cheap vs higher-quality) with a single config change and show request routing + latency delta. Success: routing change is observable in the Console logs within 30s and 90% of requests follow the new policy.
3) Demonstrate KV prefix prefetch improving tail latency for repeated conversation prefixes. Success: 30% reduction in 95th percentile token latency for repeated traces.
4) Show a rollback from canary to baseline when a simple regression is injected. Success: rollback executed and traffic returns to baseline within the configured cooldown.

High-level agenda (3-hour):
- 00:00–00:15 Setup and goals + runbook preview
- 00:15–00:45 Deploy adapter (local container) and do first end-to-end request
- 00:45–01:30 Model variant routing demo + compare metrics in Console
- 01:30–02:10 KV prefix prefetch experiment (run repeated traces, toggle prefetch)
- 02:10–02:40 Canary test + rollback exercise
- 02:40–03:00 Q&A, next steps, and action items

Quick start step-by-step (commands and small snippets) — use as live demo script:
1) Spin up adapter locally (works with the sample repo):
- git clone https://github.com/redwood-inference/workshop-adapter-template.git && cd workshop-adapter-template
- docker build -t se-sandbox-lite:latest .
- docker run -e REDWOOD_API_KEY=ephemeral_XXX -p 8080:8080 se-sandbox-lite:latest
Verify: curl -s -X POST http://localhost:8080/generate -d '{"input": "hello"}' | jq

2) Deploy to k8s (namespaced sandbox):
- kubectl apply -f k8s/namespace.yaml
- kubectl apply -f k8s/deployment-lite.yaml
- kubectl apply -f k8s/service.yaml
Check pods: kubectl get pods -n se-sandbox

3) Simple adapter config (adapter.yaml):
- routing_policy: direct
- model: redwood-llama-7b-quant
- kv_prefetch: off
- output_schema: {"assistant": "text", "confidence": "float"}
Change model to redwood-llama-7b-quant-fast for fast path during demo.

4) Toggle routing via Console draft endpoint config (demo commands):
- curl -X PATCH https://console.redwood.ai/api/v1/projects/sandbox/endpoints/chat -H 'Authorization: Bearer <admin-token>' -d '{"primary_model":"redwood-llama-7b-quant-fast","fallback_models": ["redwood-llama-7b-quant"]}'
Observe logs and metrics in Console; note averages and p95.

5) KV prefix prefetch quick experiment (toggle):
- Start with kv_prefetch: off, run repeat script: scripts/run-traces.sh --file samples/repeat-traces.json --concurrency 10
- Toggle kv_prefetch: on via adapter configmap update and rollout restart
- Re-run scripts and compare p95 token/service latencies from the adapter logs + Console traces.

Troubleshooting cheatsheet (common gotchas during workshops):
- Adapter 503 on first request: ensure REDWOOD_API_KEY is set and epoxy quota >0.
- High cold-start latency: confirm the adapter image was pre-pulled or run the warmup route to populate lazy kernels.
- KV prefetch seems ineffective: check that traces are truly reusing prefixes; synthetic traces should include repeated first-3-turn prompts.
- Canary never gets traffic: check rollout policy and that the canary label matches the service selector.

Live-debug patterns to teach the customer (commands / workflows):
- Inspect request path: curl -v to adapter -> adapter logs -> Console traces -> raw model logs.
- Inject a regression: modify adapter output schema to drop a required field; push canary and watch regression alerts in the Console.
- Rollback: use Console route rollback or kubectl rollout undo on the adapter deployment.

Sample experiment matrix to run (for the post-demo takeaway):
- Batching vs single request: run traces at 10, 50, 200 RPS and measure tokens/sec and p95 latency.
- Quant levels: compare int8 vs int4 model variant in cost and output drift.
- Prefetch TTL: try 0s/30s/120s and observe cache hit rates and memory usage.

Notes on metrics to capture live (and how to interpret):
- P95 token latency: sensitive to kernel selection and KV cache misses.
- Effective tokens-per-second and cost-per-invocation: compute from console usage tables.
- Cache hit rate: the most actionable signal for KV prefetch experiments.
- Error rate and rollbacks: correlate with commit that introduced schema change.

Follow-up deliverables to commit after workshop:
- Short playbook (1–2 pages) summarizing the chosen adapter config and the results of the three experiments above.
- GitHub PR with the sample repo changes and a Docker image tag for the customer to continue testing.
- Measurement dashboard snapshot exported from Console and a CSV of the trace runs.

Appendix A — mini adapter snippet (pseudocode):
- function handleRequest(req):
-   payload = mapToRedwoodSchema(req.body)
-   if config.kv_prefetch: warmPrefetch(payload.prefixes)
-   resp = callRedwoodAPI(payload)
-   out = mapFromRedwood(resp)
-   return out

Appendix B — workshop facilitation tips:
- Start with a concrete user story (e.g., support chat that summarizes previous purchases) rather than abstract metrics.
- Keep the first end-to-end demo tiny and guaranteed to succeed (single turn, trivial prompt).
- Use transparent noise: intentionally inject a simple failure mid-demo to show rollback discipline; customers remember recovery more than success.

Field notes and recent learnings: the lightweight-adapter pattern is potent for customers who cannot install full SDKs; the tradeoff is added-network hop cost but massive developer velocity. KV prefetch is extremely sensitive to prefix shape—small changes in user prompts make it brittle unless prompts are canonicalized server-side.

Next steps checklist for SE after session:
- Push chosen config to the customers sandbox repo and open PR.
- Attach Console dashboard snapshots to the PR and tag customer PM + infra contact.
- Propose a 2-week follow-up trial with limited Dedicated capacity if results meet success criteria.

Open questions (to capture customer decisions):
- Do they prefer adapter as a sidecar or a centralized proxy in their infra?
- Are there regulatory constraints that rule out hosted API calls?
- What SLOs (p95 latency) are non-negotiable for their product?

End of blueprint.
